from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Summary and Conclusion", [
            "Abstract spaces offer a universal language.", 
            "They bridge disparate data types.", 
            "Tools apply from AI to quantum."
        ])
        
        # Create visual elements
        arrow = Arrow(start=LEFT, end=RIGHT, color=BLUE)
        matrix = Matrix([[1, 0], [0, 1]], left_bracket="[", right_bracket="]")
        wave = FunctionGraph(lambda t: 0.5 * np.sin(3 * t), color=YELLOW)
        umbrella = Text("V", font_size=72, color=RED)
        
        # Place them
        self.place_at_grid(arrow, 'B2', 0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(matrix, 'B4', 0.5)
        self.place_at_grid(wave, 'D3', 0.8)
        self.place_in_area(umbrella, 'C3', 'D4', 1.0)
        
        self.add(arrow, matrix, wave, umbrella)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(GREEN))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        
        # Animate all previous visuals shrinking into central point
        group = VGroup(arrow, matrix, wave, umbrella)
        self.play(group.animate.scale(0.1).set_opacity(0))
        self.wait(1)

sections.title: Prerequisite Review: From Arrows to Objects
sections.content: Briefly revisit Euclidean vectors as arrows in 2D/3D space (magnitude and direction). Introduce the shift: what if a 'vector' isn't just an arrow, but a polynomial, a function, or a matrix?
sections.example: Visualize a 2D arrow vs. a sine wave f(x) = sin(x) being treated as a single 'point' in a function space.

sections.title: Defining the Arena: The 8 Axioms
sections.content: Introduce the abstract vector space as a set of objects (vectors) equipped with two operations: addition and scalar multiplication. Explain that as long as they follow the 'Rules of the Game' (Axioms like commutativity, associativity, and identity), the objects qualify as vectors.
sections.example: Analogy of a 'Universal Library': Whether the books are comic books or novels, if they follow the library's organization rules (axioms), they are all valid 'Library Contents'.

sections.title: Visualizing Abstract Spaces
sections.content: Demonstrate the abstract concept using a 'State Space' visualization. Use a character (a robot) to show that all possible configurations (position, velocity, angle) form a vector space, even if the visual doesn't look like an arrow.
sections.example: A robot moving in a grid: Its configuration vector V = [x, y, θ]. Changing the configuration follows vector addition, even if the robot isn't drawing a physical arrow.

sections.title: Concrete Application: Sound Synthesis
sections.content: Show how abstract vector spaces are applied in audio engineering. Explain that any complex sound wave is a linear combination (a vector sum) of basic sine wave vectors.
sections.example: Two birds singing: The total song is the vector sum of Bird A's frequency vector and Bird B's frequency vector within the 'Sound Vector Space'.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Reinforce that abstract vector spaces provide a universal language. They allow us to use linear algebra tools on non-spatial data, enabling everything from AI image processing to quantum mechanics.
sections.example: A final visual showing an arrow, a matrix, and a function wave converging into a single 'Vector Space' umbrella symbol.
